Neonates of the Longnose stingray (Hypanus guttatus) emerge from their mother following a period of internal development, having achieved a total length at birth of 17 cm [Lb = 17 cm]. This size at parturition is relatively modest compared to other dasyatid rays, reflecting a reproductive strategy centered on producing a small number of well-provisioned pups rather than a large litter of smaller offspring. The gestation period, which involves the young developing while nourished by yolk reserves within the maternal reproductive tract, spans approximately 213 days at a stable water temperature of 27.6 °C [T = 27.6 °C], translating to an age at birth of about 7 months [ab = about 7 months]. Our understanding of these early life-history parameters has been derived from long-term captive observations at the Ubatuba Aquarium in southeastern Brazil, where gravid females have been maintained and their parturition events closely monitored. Newborn rays are immediately capable of independent foraging, though they remain vulnerable to predation by larger teleosts and sharks during their first weeks of life in the shallow coastal nursery habitats they typically occupy.

As the juvenile stingray matures, its disc width expands considerably, with the species ultimately reaching an ultimate disc width of 98 cm [Li = 98 cm], a measurement that places it among the medium-sized members of its genus. This asymptotic body dimension is typically attained only after several years of sustained growth, with females often exceeding males in maximum disc width, a pattern of sexual size dimorphism common across many elasmobranchs. Field surveys conducted along the northeastern coast of Brazil have consistently recorded individuals approaching this maximum size in waters of moderate turbidity and depth, suggesting that the 98 cm figure represents a reliable upper bound for wild populations. The growth trajectory leading to this ultimate disc width appears to be strongly influenced by local prey availability, with individuals in productive estuarine systems reaching larger sizes more rapidly than conspecifics inhabiting oligotrophic offshore environments. This plasticity in growth underscores the species' ecological adaptability within its range across the western Atlantic, from the Caribbean to southern Brazil.

Attainment of puberty in female Longnose stingrays is marked by a disc width at puberty of 53 cm [Lp = 53 cm], a size that generally corresponds to an age of approximately 4 to 5 years based on vertebral band counts. This threshold, which can range from 50 to 56 cm, signals the onset of ovarian follicle development and the capacity for successful copulation. Males, by contrast, achieve puberty at a notably smaller disc width at puberty for males of 43.5 cm [Lp = 43.5 cm], reflecting a faster maturation schedule driven by the lower energetic costs associated with sperm production relative to gestation. This difference in size at sexual maturation between the sexes is a widespread feature in batoid fishes, where female-biased dimorphism in size at maturity is the norm. The maturation process involves testicular recrudescence in males and a progressive increase in the diameter of ovarian follicles in females, with both sexes typically becoming reproductively viable within their first few years of life in the warm coastal waters they favor.

Reproductive output in Hypanus guttatus is constrained by a relatively low fecundity and a slow breeding cycle typical of many elasmobranchs. Gravid females are known to produce between 2 and 4 pups per litter [N_R_i = between 2 and 4 pups per litter], with evidence suggesting that most individuals produce only a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year]. These values were recorded under the ambient thermal regime of their native tropical habitat, which averages 27.6 °C [T = 27.6 °C], and the maximum reprod rate implied by this combination of litter size and frequency underscores the species' inherently low intrinsic rate of increase. This conservative reproductive strategy renders the Longnose stingray particularly vulnerable to overfishing, as populations cannot quickly compensate for even moderate levels of adult mortality. The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult female can reach 21,300 grams [Wwi = 21,300 grams], a substantial body mass that supports the energetic demands of gestation and parturition, although males rarely exceed 12,000 grams in total wet weight.

Longevity in the Longnose stingray is considerable, with the maximum lifespan estimated at 13 years [am = 13 years] based on vertebral centrum annuli analysis conducted on individuals from the northeastern Brazilian continental shelf at a temperature of 27.6 °C [T = 27.6 °C]. This lifespan, measured under the prevailing sea temperature of 27.6 °C [T = 27.6 °C], positions Hypanus guttatus as a relatively long-lived batoid when compared to other members of the Dasyatidae, many of which rarely exceed a decade. The slow pace of life — late maturation, low fecundity, and extended lifespan — has important implications for the species' demographic resilience. Age-related mortality in the wild is thought to increase sharply after the 12th year, with very few individuals surviving beyond the estimated maximum lifespan. Conservation strategies for this species must therefore prioritize the protection of adult and sub-adult individuals, as the removal of even a small number of reproductive-age rays can have disproportionately large effects on the long-term viability of local populations, given the species' inherently low replacement rate.
